extracted.intended_audience: marketing researchers, AI designers, and practitioners developing consumer-facing AI
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and research-informed criteria for designing and evaluating consumer-facing AI interactions (data-capture, classification, delegation, and social experiences), with managerial recommendations to mitigate alienation and ethical harms. Also a research agenda identifying interrelationships between experience types and emergent AI experiences (learning, companionship, cyborg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms should learn how to acknowledge and accommodate the heterogeneity of human interaction styles and needs; collect information directly from consumers who have experienced alienation; leverage technology to gauge and measure alienation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize alienation using measures like amount of stress in the customer's voice in chats; interact with psychologists, sociologists, gerontologists, and other experts to learn about causes and consequences of alienation; disseminate insights throughout the organization to inform design and avoid calcifying harmful stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding harmful anthropomorphism defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of anthropomorphism should not draw on and calcify harmful stereotypes about social categories and the way they interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break with cultural conventions that idealize AI as passive/subservient (e.g., female names/voices as defaults) by involving linguists, critical theorists, and social psychologists; disseminate information about societal consequences (such as exposure to subservient female AIs) to shift designers away from harmful defaults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase effectiveness of interactive AI to minimize alienation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design interactive AI applications to reduce conversational failures and the likelihood that users feel alienated or demeaned by AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalize interactions (use the customer's name, explain reasons for malfunctions) and ensure easy and swift transitions from AI to human representatives when interactions become difficult or aversive; improving responsiveness can mitigate harmful consequences of service failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider degree of human-likeness intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether AI should be more or less humanlike given the potential to perpetuate harmful stereotypes or trigger differential reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider developing less rather than more humanlike AI (e.g., gender-neutral voices) if human-likeness reinforces stereotyping or objectification; designers must challenge the assumption that anthropomorphism always fosters better customer relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate access-equity implications when using AI for basic services
rubrics_metrics.description: When AI is used to provide welfare or essential services, designers must evaluate barriers AI might create for specific user groups even if standard performance benchmarks are satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should recognize intersectional complexities and test for differential effects on vulnerable or marginalized consumers; consider alternatives or human involvement to prevent exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design AI to facilitate human-human connection (care assemblages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than treating AI solely as a substitute for humans, design social experiences that help support connections between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strategies (similar to social media) to connect individuals to loved ones; shift the mindset from AI-as-substitute to AI-as-interface that facilitates social connection and assists human-human interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and transparency of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The timing of disclosure that the interaction partner is an algorithm may influence consumer response and the emergence of alienation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and design disclosure timing carefully (e.g., early vs. late disclosure) to avoid 'change of meaning' effects; consider situational moderators (cognitive capacity, type of disclosure) documented in related literatures on disclosure and persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and leverage brand equity as a moderator
rubrics_metrics.description: Brand attachment and equity influence consumer expectations and can insulate consumers from negative appraisals in ambiguous AI interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether strong consumer-brand relationships reduce perceptions of alienation and negative reactions; consider brand-based strategies to buffer negative effects of AI failures or controversial behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate customer-journey perspectives across AI experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand interrelationships between data-capture, classification, delegation, and social experiences rather than treating them as independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore how experience with one capability (e.g., data-capture) affects subsequent experiences (e.g., classification); design staged customer journeys (e.g., basic service with limited data followed by opt-in upgrades) to build trust and demonstrate benefits before requesting more sensitive disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalize and monitor alienation indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop measurable indicators of consumer alienation to inform design and monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include stress in customer voice during chats; firms should instrument interactions to detect when alienation is likely and trigger interventions (human handoffs, apologies, explanations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education / learning-design tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: When AI personalizes learning, designers should weigh personalization benefits against risks to learner satisfaction, motivation, and internal attribution of learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether AI-made outcomes hinder students' ability to attribute learning to their effort/talent; design personalization to support internalization and motivation rather than undermine them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess deception and substitution risks for AI companionship
rubrics_metrics.description: AI companionship (sex robots, robotic pets, companions for elderly) can provide cognitive and socioemotional benefits but also risk deceiving vulnerable users or substituting for human relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research when and how deception/substitution becomes damaging; design safeguards for vulnerable populations to avoid exploitation or harmful replacement of human contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine cyborg and embedded-AI impacts on autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: AI cyborg experiences (wearables, implants, nanorobots) emphasize hybridity and self-enhancement but can destabilize autonomy and control while also offering empowerment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate effects on consumer freedom and self-concept; consider ethical and practical tradeoffs of deeply integrated AI and develop guidelines for responsible deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research agenda: cultural and individual differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for cultural differences and individual variance in anti-bias beliefs, willingness to accept AI as social partners, and perceptions of alienation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design cross-cultural studies (e.g., Western utilitarian assistants vs. Eastern human/animal-appearing robots) and measure how cultural norms shape acceptance and perceived benefits or harms.
